title: Do Large Language Models Have Compositional Ability? An Investigation into Limitations and Scalability
authors: Zhuoyan Xu¹, Zhenmei Shi¹, Yingyu Liang¹
title_audio_script: Large language models are famously good at learning new tasks from a few in-context examples. But can they combine skills they already know? This COLM 2024 paper from the University of Wisconsin-Madison asks whether large language models have compositional ability, the capacity to solve an unseen composite task by fusing two simple tasks shown only individually. The authors build a test suite of linguistic and logical composite tasks, run it across the Llama and GPT families, and uncover a sharp dichotomy. When the two simple tasks act on separate parts of the input, models compose them well and get better with scale. When the tasks require chained, multi-step reasoning, models fail, and scaling up does not help. A theoretical analysis of linear self-attention explains exactly when composition works and when it breaks.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.necessary: Can an LLM that learns two simple tasks in-context automatically solve their composition, an unseen composite task, without ever seeing composite examples? This basic generalization is trivial for humans but largely untested for LLMs.
sections.additional: Compositional ability, solving unseen complex tasks that combine simpler ones, is viewed as essential for general intelligence, yet how LLMs handle composite tasks not seen in pretraining remains open and underexplored.
sections.audio_script: Here is the core question. Suppose a large language model has learned two simple tasks from in-context examples, capitalizing certain words and swapping certain words. If you now show it an input that needs both operations at once, can it just combine the two skills? For humans this is trivial. The surprising finding is that even GPT-4 and Claude 3 often cannot do it. So this paper asks, in a careful and controlled way, whether large language models truly have compositional ability, or whether that ability is far more limited than their individual-task performance suggests.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.necessary: LLMs excel at individual in-context tasks, but real reasoning demands fusing skills. It is unknown whether their in-context learning integrates known task abilities or fails to compose them.
sections.additional: Prior work studies compositional generalization narrowly and lacks a theoretical account of when and why composition succeeds; even GPT-4 and Claude 3 fail simple asterisk-and-parenthesis composite tasks despite solving each part.
sections.audio_script: Why look at this now? Large language models are increasingly asked to chain skills together for real reasoning, not just to repeat one operation. Yet we lack a clear account of when that chaining works. Prior studies of compositional generalization tend to be narrow and offer little theory. And the failure is easy to reproduce: give a frontier model demonstrations of two simple rules, then a test input requiring both, and it stumbles even though each rule alone is easy. That gap between per-skill competence and combined-skill failure is exactly what motivates a systematic investigation.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.necessary: The paper (1) builds a test suite of linguistic and logical composite tasks with simple tasks as in-context examples, (2) empirically reveals a dichotomy in compositional behavior across LLM families and scales, and (3) gives a theoretical analysis in a linear self-attention model explaining when composition emerges.
sections.additional: It connects the nature of a task, whether its sub-tasks act on separate input parts, to whether scaling helps, offering practical guidance on which composite tasks LLMs can be trusted to solve.
sections.audio_script: The paper makes three contributions. First, it builds a test suite of composite tasks, spanning both linguistic and logical challenges, where the in-context examples come only from the simple sub-tasks. Second, it runs this suite across the Llama and GPT families at many scales and uncovers a clear dichotomy in behavior. Third, it backs the empirical findings with theory, analyzing a linear self-attention model to explain precisely when compositional ability emerges and when scaling helps.

sections.heading: Method
sections.necessary: Under standard in-context learning (K=10 simple-task examples plus one test input), the authors evaluate four settings per composite task: each simple task alone, composite (simple-task demos, composite test), and composite in-context (composite demos, the gold-standard upper bound). They test Llama-1/2/3 and GPT families across scales on word-level and arithmetic tasks. Theoretically, they analyze a one-layer single-head linear self-attention network and show composition succeeds when the two simple tasks have "confined support", occupying separate feature subspaces of the input embedding.
sections.additional: Separable composite tasks (sub-tasks on distinct input parts) are contrasted with compose-by-step tasks (chained multi-step reasoning that shares embedding support). The theory formalizes compositional ability and links per-task accuracy gains under scale to the separable case.
sections.audio_script: The method has two halves, empirical and theoretical. Empirically, for each composite task the authors evaluate four settings under standard in-context learning with ten examples: each simple task alone, a composite setting where the demonstrations are simple tasks but the test input is composite, and a composite in-context setting where everything is composite, which acts as a gold-standard upper bound. Theoretically, they study a one-layer single-head linear self-attention network and show that composition succeeds when the two simple tasks have what they call confined support, meaning each task occupies its own separate subspace of the input embedding. When those subspaces overlap, composition breaks down.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.necessary: A custom test suite of composite tasks pairing simple building-block tasks. Linguistic tasks include Capitalization, Swap, and translation tasks (Phrase Recombination with Longer Chain; Passive-to-Active with Object-to-Subject). Logical tasks include arithmetic operations (Two Sum, Modular, Plus One) composed with word-level ones.
sections.additional: Tasks are grouped into separable composites (e.g., Capitalization & Plus One) versus compose-by-step composites (e.g., Capitalization & Swap, Modular & Two Sum Plus). Exact-match accuracy is used for logical tasks; word error rate (WER) for translation tasks.
sections.audio_script: The evaluation runs on a purpose-built test suite of composite tasks. Each composite is made from two simple building blocks. On the linguistic side there are word-level operations like capitalization and swapping, plus translation tasks such as phrase recombination with longer chains and passive-to-active with object-to-subject transformation. On the logical side there are arithmetic operations like two-sum, modular, and plus-one, combined with word-level tasks. Crucially, the tasks split into two families: separable composites, where the two operations act on different parts of the input, and compose-by-step composites, where the operations must be chained through shared reasoning. Exact-match accuracy scores the logical tasks and word error rate scores the translation tasks.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.necessary: LLMs show divergent behavior. On separable composite tasks they compose well and improve with scale, approaching the composite in-context gold standard. On compose-by-step tasks they largely fail: Llama models solve each simple task at ~90% accuracy but drop to ~20% or below on the composite, and scaling up does not help.
sections.additional: Supplying composite in-context examples restores near-simple-task accuracy, showing the models have the representation power but fail to compose it from simple-task demonstrations alone. The same composition failure appears in GPT-4 and Claude 3.
sections.audio_script: The headline result is a sharp split in behavior. On separable composite tasks, models compose the two skills well, and their accuracy climbs with scale until it approaches the gold-standard composite in-context setting. On compose-by-step tasks the picture is very different. Llama models handle each simple task at around ninety percent accuracy, yet on the composite version they collapse to roughly twenty percent or below, and making the model bigger does not help. Tellingly, if you instead give the model composite examples directly, its accuracy jumps back up. So the models clearly have the representational power to solve these tasks; what they lack is the ability to compose that power from simple-task demonstrations alone.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.necessary: Varying model scale within families cleanly separates the two regimes: on separable tasks accuracy rises with scale, while on compose-by-step tasks it stays flat or degrades. Switching from composite to composite-in-context demonstrations recovers performance, isolating composition (not capability) as the bottleneck.
sections.additional: Across word-level, arithmetic, and translation task families the same separable-vs-step dichotomy holds, and larger models improve on the composite task only when the underlying simple tasks improve, matching the confined-support scaling theory.
sections.audio_script: The scale sweep acts as the key ablation. Moving through the sizes within each model family cleanly separates the two regimes. On separable tasks, accuracy rises steadily with scale. On compose-by-step tasks, it stays flat or even degrades no matter how large the model gets. A second ablation swaps the demonstration type: replacing simple-task demonstrations with composite ones recovers performance, which isolates composition itself, not raw capability, as the bottleneck. And larger models help the composite task only when they also improve the underlying simple tasks, exactly what the confined-support theory predicts.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.necessary: - Simple tasks (capitalization / swap): ~90% accuracy for Llama families. - Compose-by-step composite task: ~20% or below, with no gain from scaling. - Separable compose-by-step examples reach 44% in (A)+(C) and 66% in (B)+(D) at larger scale.
sections.additional: In-context example count K=10; evaluated across Llama-1 (7b-65b), Llama-2 (3b-70b), Llama-3, and GPT (0.74b-6b) model scales.
sections.audio_script: A few numbers capture the story. On the simple capitalization and swap tasks, Llama models reach about ninety percent accuracy. But on the compose-by-step version of those same tasks, accuracy falls to around twenty percent or lower, and scaling the model up brings no improvement. In the milder cases, larger models climb to forty-four percent on capitalization plus two-sum and sixty-six percent on swap plus two-sum. All of this uses ten in-context examples and spans the Llama one, two, and three families and the GPT family across a wide range of parameter scales.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.necessary: LLMs can compose two skills only when the sub-tasks act on separate parts of the input; for tasks needing chained multi-step reasoning they fail and scaling does not rescue them.
sections.additional: Whether more compute helps a composite reasoning task is predictable from the task's structure: separable (confined-support) tasks scale, entangled multi-step tasks do not.
sections.audio_script: The takeaway is simple and useful. Large language models can combine two learned skills only when those skills apply to separate parts of the input. When a task instead demands genuinely chained, multi-step reasoning, the models fail to compose, and adding more parameters will not rescue them. In other words, whether extra compute helps a composite reasoning task is largely predictable from the task's structure: separable tasks scale, entangled multi-step tasks do not.
